Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was an Austrian composer who, in his tragically short life of thirty-five years, created a body of work unmatched in its scope, elegance, and emotional depth. Born in Salzburg, he was a child prodigy who mastered keyboard and violin before his adolescence and spent his career producing symphonies, concertos, operas, and chamber works that defined the Classical era. His music balances perfect formal construction with inexplicable grace, making him perhaps the most universally admired composer in the Western canon. Mozart was born in Salzburg in seventeen fifty-six and began composing and performing publicly by age five, traveling Europe as a child prodigy. He wrote his first opera at age twelve and composed continuously across all genres: forty-one symphonies, twenty-seven piano concertos, five violin concertos, and twenty-two operas. His three final symphonies, numbers thirty-nine, forty, and forty-one Jupiter, all written in seventeen eighty-eight, represent the apex of symphonic achievement in the Classical form. The Magic Flute, The Marriage of Figaro, and Don Giovanni stand among the greatest operas ever written, each showcasing different operatic modes. He combined the galant elegance of the Italian style with the rigor of Germanic counterpoint and form—a uniquely balanced achievement. Mozart struggled financially despite his genius, living an unstable life moving between Salzburg and Vienna, dependent on patrons and concert income. He died suddenly in Vienna in seventeen ninety-one, possibly of rheumatic fever, leaving the Requiem unfinished, which was completed by Franz Xaver Süssmayr.
